analysis.body:
Census BTOS provides the measured adoption figure for this nonprofit-heavy segment. In the latest period, 13.7% of firms in Other services (NAICS 81, includes grantmaking and civic organizations) answered yes to using AI in the last two weeks, up from 12.6% in the prior period. The series first asked the question in September 2023. This is a service sector that includes grantmaking and civic organizations, not a full census of every nonprofit.

Candid tracks the funding side and reports that nearly a quarter of corporate funders support using AI to decide grant approvals and denials, but for most, using AI for administrative tasks will free up time. That points to a split between back-office efficiency as the mainstream case and a smaller share of funders open to AI in grant decisions. CEP examines how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. NTEN runs sector-wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption among nonprofits. Stanford HAI's AI Index reports AI's social impact and implementation across mission-driven and public-sector organizations as the macro series.

The World of AI catalog lists four individually verified organizations: LMSYS, Khan Academy, Krita Foundation, and Blender Foundation. None are infrastructure builders in the compute or power sense. LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform. Khan Academy is an end-user of AI in education. Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software tools that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with. The catalog notes confirm only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail. It does not cover training compute providers, standards bodies, or open-model foundations.

ROI evidence is thin in these sources. Candid's administrative time framing is the closest to a reported benefit, but no ROI percentages appear. The AI Equity Project tracks accessibility, training gaps, and ethical implementation across community organizations, and it builds structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs in public libraries and community spaces. NTEN says nonprofit technology is marked by inequities within organizations and the sector that must be dismantled, and it asks practitioners to pledge to use its Equity Guide. These are governance and capacity signals rather than return on investment data. The excerpts do not describe a specific regulatory posture for nonprofit AI use.

A reader deciding whether to deploy AI in a nonprofit should treat the Census BTOS figure as a measured but modest baseline: 13.7% of firms in this nonprofit-heavy NAICS category, up from 12.6%. Funder interest is real, with Candid showing administrative use as the mainstream case and a smaller share open to AI in grant decisions. The sector's own research organizations, CEP and NTEN, focus on operations, program delivery, communications, policy adoption, and equity. The catalog of AI-focused nonprofits is small and not infrastructure-level, so the organizational picture remains narrow. Governance capacity and equitable implementation are the constraints the sources keep returning to.

https://cep.org/.brief: The Center for Effective Philanthropy page announces a limited-time discount on 2027 assessments or advisory projects, with savings up to $1000 for signing up before Sept. 30. It promotes a podcast episode where donors Jeff Atwood and Dr. Betsy Burton discuss their commitment to give away $50 million in five years. CEP describes its work offering assessments, data-driven research, customized advisory services, events, and blog commentary to influence foundations and major donors. The page also highlights new data on how nonprofits are faring and how foundations are responding, and features blog posts on topics such as inflation’s impact on grantmaking and deciding when a foundation’s mission requires more spending.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid offers a large database of grants and nonprofit information to help users locate funding opportunities, research organizations, and connect with funders. According to Candid, about 25 % of corporate funders use AI to decide grant approvals and denials. For most funders, Candid reports that “using AI for administrative tasks will free up time.” The site emphasizes its comprehensive data as a resource for those seeking funding or researching nonprofits.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project says it creates structured learning routes and cross-generational programs intended to make artificial intelligence accessible, ethical, and practical for all communities. It describes turning public libraries and community spaces into interactive learning settings where older adults and student volunteers work together on practical AI tools. The organization states it runs a global network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented communities, with support structures meant to ensure every student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. It also mentions an International AI for Impact Challenge that asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world problems, with top participants gaining lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page reports that four organizations, two nonprofits and two open-source foundations, steer AI tools and evaluation infrastructure, but none build compute infrastructure. LMSYS manages the “Chatbot Arena” platform, a neutral evaluation tool used by the AI community to benchmark model quality. Khan Academy applies AI in education, while the Krita and Blender Foundations maintain creative software that increasingly intersects with AI-generated imagery and 3D content. The page notes it does not cover training compute providers, standards bodies, or open-model foundations, and that the information is limited to organizational structure and nonprofit status, offering no insight into funding or governance.
